title: Course Structure and Policies
markdown:
## What this covers

This chapter is the syllabus of Berkeley's Stat 243, *Statistical Computing*, as stated by the
course itself rather than by an outside description. It answers "what is this course, how is it
run, and how am I graded", by combining the syllabus pages from three consecutive offerings — fall
2024, fall 2025, and fall 2026 — into one account and noting where the course's own answer to that
question changed. There is no mathematics here to derive; the point of this chapter is to make the
logistics and grading legible before the content chapters, and to show how the instructor's stance
on AI-assisted problem sets moved year over year.

## What the course is, and what it is not

Stat 243 is an introduction to statistical computing taught in Python — with, from fall 2025
onward, "statistical" defined broadly enough to include data science and machine learning. It has
two strands: **programming concepts** (data and text manipulation, regular expressions, data
structures, functions and variable scope, memory use, efficiency, debugging, testing, parallel
processing) and **statistical computing concepts** (working with large datasets, numerical linear
algebra, computer arithmetic and precision, simulation and Monte Carlo methods, numerical
optimization). It also covers the basics of UNIX/Linux — shell scripting and working on remote
servers — and touches R.

The syllabus is explicit about what the course is *not*: it is not a course on learning Python for
its own sake (Python is the vehicle, not the subject), and it is not a course on specific
statistical, machine-learning, or data-analysis methods. The stated goal is that its computing
content complement, rather than duplicate, the models and methods taught elsewhere in the
statistics/biostatistics graduate curriculum.

**Prerequisites** are informal: a background in calculus, linear algebra, probability, and
statistics, basic ability to use a computer (no UNIX shell experience assumed), and Python at the
level of the department's pre-course computing-skills workshop. Students without that Python
background are told to expect to spend the first couple of weeks catching up.

In fall 2026 the course was split for the first time into two linked half-semester, two-credit
courses — **Stat 243A** (programming concepts) and **Stat 243B** (numerical computing) — and the
prerequisites split with it: 243A assumes the workshop-level Python; 243B assumes comfort with
calculus and linear algebra and with programming in Python, but not necessarily at the 243A level,
i.e. 243B does not strictly require having taken 243A.

## Objectives

By the end of the course (or, from 2026, by the end of both half-courses), a student should be able
to:

- operate effectively in a UNIX environment and on remote servers and compute clusters;
- program effectively, with a solid grasp of general programming concepts and an advanced knowledge
  of Python;
- use tools and practices for reproducible research and good scientific computing; and
- understand and apply numerical precision, numerical linear algebra, optimization, and simulation
  to statistics- and data-science problems.

("Numerical precision" was added to this last objective from fall 2025 on; the substance is the
same set of numerical-computing topics in all three years.)

## Topics, and how they were reorganised in 2026

Fall 2024 and fall 2025 taught the same twelve-topic sequence, in the same order, with the same
rough day-counts:

1. Introduction to UNIX, operating on a compute server (1 day)
2. Data formats, data access, webscraping, data structures (2 days)
3. Debugging, good programming practices, reproducible research (1 day)
4. The bash shell and shell scripting, version control (3 days)
5. Advanced Python programming: text processing and regular expressions, object-oriented
   programming, functions and variable scope, memory use, efficient programming (9 days)
6. Parallel processing (2 days)
7. Working with databases, hashing, and big data (3 days)
8. Computer arithmetic and representation of numbers on a computer (3 days)
9. Simulation studies and Monte Carlo (2 days)
10. Numerical linear algebra (5 days)
11. Optimization (5 days)
12. Graphics (1 day)

Fall 2026 kept the same content but reordered and re-partitioned it across the two new
half-courses, and dropped the graphics unit while adding one on optimization for deep learning:

| Stat 243A (programming) | days | Stat 243B (numerical computing) | days |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Introduction to UNIX, compute servers | 1 | Computer arithmetic / number representation | 3 |
| Bash shell, shell scripting, version control | 3 | Simulation studies and Monte Carlo | 2 |
| Debugging, good practices, reproducibility | 1 | Numerical linear algebra | 4 |
| Advanced Python: text/regex, OOP, scope, memory, efficiency | 9 | Optimization | 6 |
| Databases, hashing, big data | 3 | Optimization for deep learning | 2 |
| Parallel processing | 2 | | |
| Data formats, access, webscraping, data structures | 2 | | |

Numerical linear algebra lost a day and optimization gained one relative to the combined course,
and the new deep-learning-optimization unit is the one genuinely new topic across the three years.

## Running the course

**Communication** goes through the course's Ed Discussion site — students are told to route
content questions there rather than by email, so that the GSI's or instructor's answer benefits
everyone, and to turn on email notifications since Ed Discussion is also the channel for
announcements. Course materials live on the GitHub-Pages course website and its GitHub repository;
video (recorded lectures, via bCourses' Media Gallery) is the one thing kept off the main site.
Assignments are submitted and graded through Gradescope (renamed Pensive/Gradescope in fall 2026).

**Sections** are GSI-led, two hours, twice a week (two sections offered; the earlier one is
consistently oversubscribed, so students are asked to attend their assigned section). From fall
2025 on, part of section time is used for the new in-section problem-set quizzes (below); in 2024,
section content was demonstrations, group work, paper discussion, and problem-set review.

**Computing resources**: most work is fine on a personal laptop; later problem sets use the
Statistics Department's Linux cluster, the SCF JupyterHub, or the campus DataHub (the syllabus
flags DataHub as too resource-limited for the more computationally heavy later work). Required
software is the UNIX/bash shell, Git, Python (Miniforge/Conda recommended), and Quarto for writing
up assignments; VS Code was added to the list from fall 2025, becoming used "extensively" by fall
2026.

**Personnel**: Chris Paciorek has taught all three offerings; the GSI changed from João Vitor
Romano (2024, 2025) to Reece Huff (2026).

## Course materials

The primary material is the course's own notes on the course website/GitHub, plus SCF (Statistical
Computing Facility) tutorials. No single textbook is required; the syllabus lists back-up
references for particular parts of the course:

- bash: Newham and Rosenblatt, *Learning the bash Shell*
- Quarto: the official Quarto reference guide
- statistical computing generally: Gentle, *Computational Statistics*; Gentle, *Matrix Algebra* (or
  *Numerical Linear Algebra with Applications in Statistics*)
- more detail on specific topics: Lange, *Numerical Analysis for Statisticians*; Monahan,
  *Numerical Methods of Statistics*
- from fall 2025: Irving, Hertweck, Johnston, Ostblom, Wickham, and Wilson, *Research Software
  Engineering with Python*, for Python/bash/Git/software-skills material generally

## Grading, and how the design changed

**Fall 2024** split the grade as 50% problem sets, 25% on two in-person quizzes, 15% on a final
group project, and 10% on class participation (in-class Google-forms responses, occasional non-PS
assignments, and substantive Ed Discussion contribution). Each problem set was scored 0–3 on each
of three components — presentation/explanation, technical accuracy, and code quality — against a
published qualitative rubric, with the total a weighted sum of the three.

**Fall 2025** introduced a **problem-set quiz**: a short, closed-book, paper quiz given in section
very soon after each problem set is due, testing understanding of a subset of the problems
directly. A student who understood the material was expected to do well without separately
studying for it. A poor result could be appealed through an oral retake with the instructor. The
grading weights moved to reflect this — 45% problem sets, split into 15% completion and 30%
in-section quizzes; 30% on two mini-exams (replacing the old quizzes); 15% project; 10%
participation — and the per-component problem-set score was simplified from a 0–3 to a 0–2
(no/partial/full credit) scale, because the quizzes, not the write-up, were now doing the job of
assessing technical understanding.

The syllabus frames this explicitly as a response to generative AI: think of the problem set and
its quiz together as a **train/test split**. Students have latitude in how they work the "training"
problem set — including using AI tools or classmates — but a strategy that amounts to overfitting
to that help (copying an AI's or a classmate's answer without understanding it) shows up as poor
performance on the "test", the quiz, which cannot be prepared for except by understanding the
material.

**Fall 2026** kept the train/test framing and the 0–2 problem-set scoring, but restructured around
the 243A/243B split: each half-course carries its own single mini-exam (243A on 12 October, 243B on
23 November) rather than two, and the **final group project was dropped** — the fall-2026 grading
page has no project component at all. Weights became 55% problem sets (20% completion, 35%
in-section quizzes), 35% on the one mini-exam, and 10% participation. The retake procedure gained
an explicit limit: a student should use it "once or twice" at most, and not for a point or two.

## Problem sets, collaboration, and the AI policy

Mechanically, problem-set rules were stable across all three years: assignments are written in
Quarto; submission is both a PDF to Gradescope by the start of class on the due date *and* the PDF,
code, and Quarto source pushed to the student's class GitHub repository, with on-time status judged
by the Gradescope timestamp. Prose should state the goal and strategy before the code — "raw code
without explanation is not an appropriate solution" — with function definitions kept in a separate
`.py` file and lengthy code in an appendix. Mathematical derivations may be handwritten and scanned.

What moved is the stance on getting help, in step with the mini-exam/quiz redesign above:

- **Fall 2024**: working with others is encouraged, but a submitted solution must be one's own.
  Sharing is limited to discussing approaches and at most a line of syntax; complete code or
  solutions may not be shared or requested. ChatGPT-style tools are allowed for small pieces of a
  problem, not whole questions, and any idea taken from a classmate or a chatbot must be
  attributed; a "Collaboration" section listing anyone consulted is a required part of every
  submission.
- **Fall 2025 and 2026**: the instructor states he is "not going to police" AI use and explicitly
  welcomes both AI tools and classmate collaboration, but frames the trade-off directly: turning in
  what is mostly an AI's or classmate's answer will show up on the quiz/mini-exam. The suggested
  discipline is to attempt a problem substantially alone first, use AI or others for small checked
  pieces, and only lean on them more fully once genuinely stuck — attribution is still required
  (in a code comment for small syntax borrowings), but the separate "Collaboration" section is no
  longer required, since the quiz rather than the write-up is what has to reflect the student's own
  understanding.

## Academic honesty

All three syllabi close with the campus Honor Code — "As a member of the UC Berkeley community, I
act with honesty, integrity, and respect for others" — and a note from the instructor that the
problem-set collaboration and AI rules above are how that code is meant to be read for this course.
The Honor Code text itself is unchanged across years except that the fall-2025 and fall-2026
versions add "with regard to AI" to the pointer back to the instructor's own rules. It covers
cheating and plagiarism in the usual terms: quizzes and mini-exams are closed-book and individual;
copying another's work or ideas without attribution is plagiarism; and violations are referred to
the campus Center for Student Conduct.

## Sources

This chapter is built entirely from syllabus "notes" pages — no slides, transcript, or problem sets
were supplied for it. Six pages per year, all CC BY 4.0, converted from each year's `syllabus.qmd`:

- **Fall 2024** — `berkeley-stat243/fall-2024`, commit `9c62305`: `01-course-description.md`
  through `06-campus-honor-code.md`.
- **Fall 2025** — `berkeley-stat243/fall-2025`, commit `035a19e`: the same six pages.
- **Fall 2026** — `berkeley-stat243/fall-2026`, commit `c74395e`: the same six pages, including the
  243A/243B split introduced that year.

Every grading percentage, prerequisite, topic list, and policy quoted or paraphrased above is drawn
directly from these eighteen pages.
